outages.cause: Rolling and emergency blackouts after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, including a large-scale attack on Nov 20 and further strikes reported on Nov 21, Nov 22, and Nov 23. Ukrenergo, as reported Tuesday evening by UNN, kurs.com.ua, 24tv.ua, and UNIAN, said planned outage schedules would again be in effect around the clock on Wednesday, Nov 25, in parts of the country, with hourly outages of 0.5 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers and capacity-limitation schedules for industry. kurs.com.ua, citing Ukrenergo, said that Tuesday's hourly outages had ranged from 0.5 to 3.5 queues, and that the maximum amount of restrictions on Wednesday would decrease by half a queue. UNIAN, in a Tuesday evening update, also published regional Wednesday schedules, including all-day outages in Poltava region and lighter, once-a-day outages in Lviv region. Suspilne, in a Wednesday morning, Nov 25 report, citing Ukrenergo, said consumption restrictions remained in effect on Wednesday in Dnipropetrovsk region and in parts of Ukraine, with schedules applied throughout the day, and that the situation could change. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, in a Tuesday, Nov 24 morning update reported by UNN, Interfax-Ukraine, and Ukrainska Pravda, said Russian forces continued attacking energy infrastructure over the past day. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as reported by UNN, said last night the Russians focused their strikes on electricity distribution and transmission infrastructure in Zhytomyr region, and that the electricity situation was difficult in Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih, Pavlohrad, and other cities and communities. Hromadske Radio, in a Nov 24 report, said Russian forces had attacked civilian and energy infrastructure in Zhytomyr region over Nov 23 and into the night, and that on the morning of Tuesday, Nov 24, they attacked the north of Rivne region, with energy facilities under attack. The Energy Ministry also said adverse weather had left 176 settlements in Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy, and Poltava regions without electricity as of Tuesday morning

UNN, citing Ukrenergo, said one group means four hours without electricity, so Wednesday outages may last from two to 12 hours. kurs.com.ua, citing Ukrenergo, said that on Tuesday, Nov 24, the volume of hourly outages had ranged from 0.5 to 3.5 queues, and that the maximum amount of restrictions on Wednesday would therefore decrease by half a queue. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported by UNN at 9:48 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (1:48 a.m. CT), by Interfax-Ukraine at 11:22 a.m. Tuesday (3:22 a.m. CT), citing First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov at a Tuesday briefing, and by Ukrainska Pravda at 11:25 a.m. Tuesday (3:25 a.m. CT), said that as of the morning of Tuesday, Nov 24, some consumers in Zhytomyr, Zaporizhzhia, Rivne, Kharkiv, and Chernihiv regions remained without electricity as a result of Russian attacks on energy infrastructure over the past day, and that emergency outages were being imposed in Kharkiv region because of equipment damage from earlier attacks and reduced voltage in the high-voltage network, with a return to predictable schedules possible once the situation in the power system stabilizes. UNN, Interfax-Ukraine, and Ukrainska Pravda, citing the ministry and Ukrenergo, also said that throughout Tuesday, Nov 24, hourly electricity-outage schedules were in effect in most regions, that capacity-limitation schedules applied to industry, and that, according to Ukrenergo, hourly schedules in some regions applied around the clock to all categories of consumers, from 0.5 to 3.5 queues. outages.cause: Repeated Russian attacks on high-voltage transmission networks and other energy facilities critical to the region, including a strike on a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi energy facility on the morning of Nov 20. On Monday, Nov 23, Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper said scheduled power-outage timetables were being reinstated in place of emergency blackouts after energy workers restored damaged infrastructure, and DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi said repairs had made a return to stabilization schedules possible, while warning that the energy system remained vulnerable to significant loads. Tuesday sources said those stabilization schedules remained in effect on Nov 24. Odesa Report, in a Tuesday evening, Nov 24 report, said that in Odesa and Odesa district energy workers had already returned to stabilization schedules after difficult emergency repairs, while networks remained vulnerable to overloads, and that hourly schedules would again be applied on Wednesday, Nov 25. Odesa Report and Odessa Life, citing DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, said that on Wednesday, Nov 25, from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., urgent equipment repairs would leave part of Odesa's Peresypskyi district without electricity, and that the work period may be extended if an air-raid alert is declared
outages.affected: Odesa Report, in a report published at 10:02 p.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (2:02 p.m. CT), citing Ukrenergo, said that on Wednesday, Nov 25, hourly outage schedules would be applied throughout the day, and that, depending on the region, electricity may be absent from two to 12 hours a day, with 0.5 to 3 queues of restrictions for household consumers and separate capacity-limitation schedules for industry, because of the aftermath of Russian attacks. The same report said that in Odesa and Odesa district, energy workers had already returned to stabilization schedules after difficult emergency repairs, while networks remained vulnerable to overloads, so schedules could be adjusted depending on the state of the energy system, and that residents should check the exact time for a given address on the website or chatbots of DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi. Odesa Report and Odessa Life, citing DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, also said that on Wednesday, Nov 25, from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., energy workers would carry out urgent equipment repairs, during which part of Odesa's Peresypskyi district would be without electricity, that the work period may be extended if an air-raid alert is declared, and that after the repairs are completed electricity would be restored gradually. Ukrenergo, as published by Malva.TV at 7:49 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (11:49 p.m. CT Monday), said overnight restoration work had continued in Odesa region, where energy infrastructure had been significantly damaged by Russian attacks, that the situation in Odesa region had been partially stabilized, and that electricity supply to critical infrastructure in Odesa had been restored. Novyny.LIVE, at 9:31 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (1:31 a.m. CT), citing DTEK, said DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi was applying hourly stabilization-outage schedules in Odesa and the region on Tuesday, Nov 24, through 12:00 a.m., that outages were assigned by group, and that the schedule could change depending on the state of the energy system; the same report said tram and trolleybus service in Odesa had resumed after the widespread blackout, with average intervals of 15 to 20 minutes, and that from 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Tuesday repair work in the Peresypskyi district would de-energize traction substations feeding tram routes 1 and 7 on a named section. OdesaVoice, in a Nov 24 report, citing First Deputy Mayor Oleksandr Filatov, said electricity supply to all critically important infrastructure in Odesa had been restored after two days of outages caused by strikes on main transmission networks, that water supply and wastewater systems were fully operating in all districts of the city, that all district and small boiler houses had been restored, that heat had begun to reach hospitals, educational institutions, other social facilities, and residential buildings, and that schools and kindergartens that had heat restored on Nov 23 would operate in the normal mode on Nov 24; the same report said 27 social buses were running to supplement trolleybuses and trams, and that about 300 Points of Invincibility were operating in the city. Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper, as reported by LB.ua at 8:03 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (12:03 p.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), had said that in Odesa and Odesa District, scheduled power-outage timetables were being reinstated in place of emergency blackouts, that the return to planned schedules had become possible because of continuous work by energy workers restoring damaged infrastructure, and that residents were being urged to use electricity sparingly so as not to overload the power system and cause new emergency outages. DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, in a Nov 23 statement on its website, said that thanks to difficult repairs and the restoration of equipment, energy workers had been able to return to stabilization schedules, that the energy system remained vulnerable to significant loads, and that customers should not turn on all electrical appliances at once when power returned, in order to avoid overloading the networks and causing new accidents. An earlier Monday statement by Kiper, as reported by Censor.NET at 12:35 p.m. EET Monday, Nov 23 (4:35 a.m. CT), by UNN at 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday (2:11 a.m. CT), and by Slovo i Dilo at 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (4:38 a.m. CT), had said the electricity-supply situation in Odesa region remained difficult but that measures were being taken to stabilize it; that emergency outages without schedules were still being applied because the damaged equipment could not yet supply all consumers at once; that all critical infrastructure and some consumers had already been energized; that water was available in all districts, with possible pumping interruptions in some apartment buildings; that 9 of 11 large boiler houses were operating, with 2 more plus the CHP being brought online; that heat had already been supplied to 186,000 subscribers; and that about 79,000 consumers remained temporarily without heating. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as reported by UNN at 9:48 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (1:48 a.m. CT), said he was grateful to everyone working in Odesa and the region, repairing the networks and ensuring alternative supply routes. The latest published Tuesday stabilization-outage schedules from DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, as reported earlier Tuesday by Novyny.LIVE, remained the most recent official Odesa-area schedule found as of this check. outages.place: Dnipro, Samar, and parts of Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dniprovskyi, Samar, Pavlohrad, Synelnykove, and Kamianske districts
outages.cause: Russian attacks on four DTEK energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast over Nov 21 and Nov 22, according to earlier DTEK accounts, which said most of the facilities had been struck before, that equipment was damaged and fires broke out at several sites, and that damage to main transmission networks meant not all consumers could yet be reconnected. DTEK, as reported by NV at 8:25 p.m. Tuesday, Nov 24, and by kurs.com.ua, said that on Tuesday, by order of Ukrenergo, emergency power outages were in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohrad, Synelnykove, and Samar districts, where previously published hourly schedules were not being applied, and that the situation remained difficult because of damage to main transmission networks. Suspilne, in a Wednesday morning, Nov 25 report, citing DTEK, said emergency outages remained in effect on Wednesday in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, where schedules were not being applied, and, citing Ukrenergo, that consumption restrictions were in effect in the region throughout the day. Informator, citing Ukrenergo, later published approximate DTEK group schedules for Wednesday, Nov 25, that it said would apply if emergency outages were not in effect in Dnipro and the region
outages.affected: Suspilne, in a report published at 7:32 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (11:32 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24), and updated at 7:51 a.m. Wednesday (11:51 p.m. CT Tuesday), citing Ukrenergo, said that on Wednesday, Nov 25, electricity-consumption restrictions were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk region and in parts of Ukraine, that schedules for all categories of consumers were being applied throughout the day, and that the situation could change. The same report, citing DTEK, said emergency outages had been introduced in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, and that schedules were not in effect there. Suspilne also published Wednesday hourly outage schedules for customers of the Central Energy Company (CEK) and a separate Wednesday schedule for some Pavlohrad customers who were temporarily being switched off on a separate timetable, and it said DTEK customers could check outage hours on the company's website. DTEK, as reported by NV at 8:25 p.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (12:25 p.m. CT) and by kurs.com.ua, said that on Tuesday, Nov 24, by order of Ukrenergo, emergency power outages had been introduced in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohrad, Synelnykove, and Samar districts of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, and that previously published hourly schedules were not in effect in those areas. DTEK said the electricity-supply situation in the region remained difficult because of damage to main transmission networks, that electricity had already been restored to critical-infrastructure facilities, and that energy workers were continuing repairs to restore supply to homes as quickly as possible, with the work complicated by prolonged air-raid alerts. NV, citing DTEK, also said that over Nov 22-23 Russian forces had attacked four DTEK energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, after which about 353,000 households had been left without electricity, including a significant part of Dnipro, Samar, and adjacent districts. Informator, citing Ukrenergo, said that on Wednesday, Nov 25, hourly outage schedules would be in effect in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast around the clock, from 12:00 a.m. to 11:59 p.m., with 0.5 to 3 queues applied at a time nationwide and capacity limits for industry, and it published approximate DTEK group schedules for Wednesday that it said would apply if emergency outages were not in effect in Dnipro and the region. No later official DTEK account was found confirming that those emergency outages had already been lifted. Ukrenergo, as published by Malva.TV at 7:49 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (11:49 p.m. CT Monday), said overnight restoration work had continued in Dnipropetrovsk region, where energy infrastructure had been significantly damaged by Russian attacks, that the situation there remained significantly more difficult, that hourly outage schedules were in effect in the region, and that energy workers were continuing work in order to reduce the volume of restrictions as quickly as possible. The Dnipro City Council, in a statement dated 7:17 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (11:17 p.m. CT Monday), said that because traction substations feeding the electric-transport contact network had been de-energized, tram and trolleybus service had been partially suspended, and that as of 7:00 a.m. Tuesday (11:00 p.m. CT Monday) tram routes 1, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, and 19 were suspended, tram route 5 was running on a shortened route, many trolleybus routes including ring B were suspended, some trolleybus routes including ring A were running, and the metro was operating on a weekend schedule. Dnepr.info, at 11:06 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (3:06 a.m. CT), said disruptions to electric transport were continuing, with some tram and trolleybus routes then running full or shortened routes and a number of routes still suspended. DTEK, as reported by Kyiv Independent in an article dated 9:19 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (1:19 p.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), by NV at 3:46 p.m. Monday, Nov 23 (7:46 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), and by Delo.ua, said Russian attacks on four of its energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast over two days, Nov 21 and Nov 22, had left about 353,000 households without electricity. Those reports, citing DTEK, said a significant part of Dnipro, the city of Samar, and adjacent districts had been left without power; that the facilities were hit in Dnipro and surrounding areas, damaging equipment and causing fires at several sites; that most of the facilities had been struck before; and that no energy workers were injured in the recent attacks. DTEK said emergency repair crews had worked through the night and were continuing restoration efforts, prioritizing electricity supplies to critical infrastructure, but that damage to main transmission networks meant technicians could not yet reconnect all consumers, and it did not give a timeline for restoring power to all affected households. Emergency power cuts were in effect in Dnipro and the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, with regular outage schedules suspended there; other parts of the region were subject to scheduled cuts ordered by Ukrenergo. An earlier Monday morning account from Ukrenergo, as reported by UNN at 10:11 a.m. Kyiv time Monday, Nov 23 (2:11 a.m. CT) and by Slovo i Dilo at 12:38 p.m. EET Monday (4:38 a.m. CT), had said the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast situation remained significantly more difficult, with hourly outage schedules in effect and overnight restoration work after significant damage from Russian attacks. Dnipropetrovsk regional council head Mykola Lukashuk, via Vidomo at 10:59 a.m. Monday (2:59 a.m. CT if Kyiv time / EET), had said emergency outages remained in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianske, and Pavlohrad districts, where DTEK hourly schedules were not being applied, with an hourly schedule in effect for Central Energy Company (CEK) customers and a separate schedule for part of Pavlohrad. Dniprovska Poradnytsia (dnpr.com.ua), in a report published at 1:35 p.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (5:35 a.m. CT), citing DTEK, said that as of 1:05 p.m. Tuesday (5:05 a.m. CT), emergency outages were in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Kamianskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts, that schedules were not being applied in those areas, and that stabilization outages by schedule were in effect in the rest of the region. That report said customers who were de-energized at about 12:00 p.m. were planned to have service restored by 5:30 p.m., and that for groups 5.1 and 5.2 still without power because of emergency outages, restoration was expected at about 4:30 p.m., with power to be returned gradually and all times described as approximate and subject to change. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as reported by UNN at 9:48 a.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (1:48 a.m. CT), said there were reports on the electricity situation in Dnipropetrovsk region, in Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih, Pavlohrad, and other cities and communities, and that the electricity situation was difficult but the necessary forces had been engaged to restore it. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Tuesday morning by UNN, Interfax-Ukraine, and Ukrainska Pravda, also said adverse weather had left 176 settlements in Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy, and Poltava regions without electricity as of Tuesday morning. The earlier DTEK figure of about 353,000 households without electricity, reported by Kyiv Independent on Monday evening, was not updated with a later official household count in the Tuesday afternoon DTEK account found for this check. No later official regional household count was found as of 11:55 PM CT Tuesday, Nov 24 (7:55 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, EET).

outages.place: Kurdistan Region, including Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok, Bazian, and Chamchamal
outages.cause: Suspected drone attack on the Khor Mor gas field on the night of Nov 8, 2026, which halted gas production that supplies much of the region's electricity generation. Dana Gas, the field's operator, later said the facility had sustained significant damage and could produce no gas
outages.affected: The New Region, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, said gas production at the Khor Mor field was expected to resume in the coming days after a Monday meeting of delegations from Erbil and Baghdad with the field's operator, Dana Gas; that, according to information acquired by The New Region, the outcome of the meeting was positive, with Dana Gas set to resume gas production in the next two to three days; and that a source at the field told The New Region that all employees at Khor Mor had returned to work, that Dana Gas was set to release a statement on the resumption of operations in the near future, that efforts to repair the damaged sections were also expected to begin soon, and that production was expected to resume within the next 48 hours in areas unaffected by the attack. Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry, told The New Region on Monday that electricity generation at power stations was expected to resume within hours of gas production restarting, with supply gradually increasing, but that it could take up to 24 hours of normal operations for electricity production to return to pre-attack levels. Those reports did not say that Khor Mor production or pre-attack electricity supply had already resumed. outages.cause: Drone attacks on power stations and other electricity infrastructure during the war between the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces
outages.affected: No official customer count. Drop Site News, in a Nov 20, 2026 report from Khartoum, said a particularly intense wave of drone strikes at the end of October and into November targeting power stations, fuel supplies, and electricity infrastructure had brought the country's power grid to the brink of collapse, and that two weeks after the wave of attacks, major substations remained out of service. Shaker Ismail, an engineer with the Sudanese Electricity Company, told Drop Site that repairing some of the country's most important power facilities could take months or longer, that high-capacity transformers and digital control systems had been damaged, and that replacement transformers must be manufactured to order abroad. Ismail said the Um Dabakir thermal power plant in White Nile State was badly damaged in an Oct 29 strike and forced to shut down, and that the Al-Markhiyat substation west of Omdurman was put out of service after an Oct 27 strike; he said affected areas continued to experience prolonged outages and scheduled power cuts as of this week. The report said the Sudan Electricity Holding Company and Ministry of Energy had yet to publicly announce the restoration of the major facilities damaged in the attacks. A United Nations report published Nov 17, issued in Geneva and posted on the UN in Sudan website, said that in just over two weeks between Oct 20 and Nov 4, 29 drone strikes, attributed to the Rapid Support Forces, hit electricity facilities and fuel stations across 11 states, triggering widespread power blackouts and further fuel shortages affecting millions far from the conflict frontlines. An earlier Al Jazeera Nov 15 feature said there is no clear schedule for the resulting power cuts, which can last anywhere between six hours and a day, and, citing The Associated Press, said repeated drone attacks on power stations have seen electricity generation fall from about 4,400 megawatts before the war to about 1,100 MW. Residents and a small-business owner in Port Sudan described prolonged, unreliable cuts, including outages lasting more than 24 hours. Al-Ghad Al-Sudani, in a report last updated Nov 22, 2026, said explosions and drone flights returned to Khartoum on Sunday morning, Nov 22, amid reports of attacks on military sites in various parts of the capital, and that the attacks coincided with power outages in large parts of the city; the report did not give a customer count or independently establish the cause of that outage. Democracy Now, in a Nov 24, 2026 headline, said Sudan's military reported intercepting drones launched by the Rapid Support Forces over Khartoum after attacks that struck the city's main airport and several buildings, including a U.N. facility, and that those attacks came as Sudan's power grid was on the brink of collapse following attacks on electricity stations; that headline did not state that the Nov 24 drone activity itself had struck power stations or give a customer count. No later official national customer count or official restoration timetable was found as of 11:55 PM CT Tuesday, Nov 24 (7:55 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, Sudan time).
